paragraphs: Yaddua the Babylonian (Yaddua, Nehemiah 3:7, as cited).

A Tanna mentioned once, according to Hyman, in Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:9. He reports in Rabbi Meir’s name that an attack from one direction does not count as an unavoidable loss, while an attack from two directions does.

notes.text: The supplied Nehemiah locator is 3:7. The consulted verse names Yadon rather than Yaddua, so the Biblical parenthesis remains a source question and is not identified with the Tanna.

The supplied biblical locator פג-ז is conventionally rendered3:7, while the earlier consulted verse names Yadon rather than Yaddua. Other Nehemiah names do not settle the intended verse, and the parenthesis is not identified with this Tanna. פ״א means once; רוח is direction of attack and אונס concerns unavoidable loss in bailee liability, with one-direction negation and two-direction assertion preserved. No new Mishnah witness is bound this pass, so the abbreviated Meir title remains R'.

Hyman’s printed parenthesis (vol. II, p. 533) gives Nehemiah פג-ז. The consulted Nehemiah 3:7 names Yadon the Meronothite. Nehemiah 12:11 and 12:22 have the name Yaddua in different contexts, so the intended reference remains uncertain. Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:9 names Yaddua the Babylonian and attributes the distinction to Rabbi Meir in the case of two dogs.
